The United States should not adopt a universal basic income. A true UBI—regular, unconditional cash to every adult citizen—fails basic tests of fiscal sustainability, incentives, and evidence. Even a modest $1,000 monthly payment to 250 million adults would cost roughly $3 trillion per year before any administrative overhead. That figure exceeds current combined spending on Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid and would require either enormous new taxes, large cuts to other programs, or continued deficit expansion at a moment when federal debt already exceeds 120 percent of GDP and major entitlements face insolvency. Taxes of that magnitude create deadweight losses that shrink the very tax base needed to fund the program; money-printing simply produces inflation that erodes the real value of the transfer, especially for housing, food, and energy.

Work incentives matter. Labor-force participation has already declined for prime-age men; an unconditional check large enough to matter would further reduce hours worked, particularly among lower-skilled workers. Small-scale pilots (Finland’s limited experiment, Stockton, certain tribal dividends) do not refute this: they are neither universal, permanent, nor large enough to substitute for wages, and they often retain other safety-net programs. Historical analogues—disability expansions, long-term unemployment insurance, and Native American casino payments—show measurable drops in employment and delayed human-capital investment. Replacing the existing patchwork of welfare with a single check sounds administratively attractive, yet political reality is additive, not substitutive; the result is higher total spending and weaker work requirements.
